whereisthezeitgeist?editing office.title: Close Remote关闭遥控
whereisthezeitgeist?editing office.artist: Matthias Kaiser, Yan Jun (颜峻）,Reinhold Friedl, Nicola Hein,Kai Winter,Sabine Worthmann
whereisthezeitgeist?editing office.about:
In a world that shares its images of horror with us on a scale never before seen in human history, our eyes are becoming increasingly dulled. One minute we're watching an aeroplane break in two and burst into flames as it lands; the next we're up close (thanks to various bodycams) to guards in an American prison inflicting fatal injuries on a prisoner who is unable to defend himself; and seconds later we're stumbling through a bombed-out city in Lebanon.
The list goes on and on; as we all know, the darker timelines never seem to take a break.
What does this have to do with the music of Matthias Kaiser, Yan Jun, Reinhold Friedl, Nicola Hein, Kai Winter and Sabine Worthmann?
Nothing and everything. We will experience it.
For the three compositions on ‘Close Remote’, Kaiser, Jun, Friedl, Hein, Winter and Worthmann met at Studio Zentrifuge in Berlin on 22 July 2022 to develop a programme involving electronics, inside piano, prepared and amplified violin, saxophone, bass and feedback in dialogue over the course of an afternoon (which says a lot about the artists' understanding of time) and perform it in front of an audience that evening.
The recording of this set is now available as ‘Close Remote’. I decided not to let all the information mentioned above get to me at first, but only to include it after I had written the actual text, so that I could listen to the music without any visual cues, so to speak.
„Breath Signals“ / „Remote Connectivity / „Close Isolation“
‘Close Remote’ sounds impressively ominous, not just gloomy, but downright threatening, even fatal.
The first piece, ‘Breath Signals’, wraps itself around us listeners, takes away the air we breathe, and puts us in a state of fear that cannot be denied, just as one does with the flood of imagery by closing one's eyes to it. Sound eats the soul, to paraphrase Rainer Werner Fassbinder.
In the second half of the 13-minute piece, the dark grey mood becomes even darker until the meandering noise of the drone symphony seems to take on a voice whose embodiment evokes associations with ES, the ultimate evil from the sewers of Steven King's civilisation.
In the digital economy, there is the term ‘remote closer’, a person who conducts business without being physically present. Matthias Kaiser, Yan Jun, Reinhold Friedl, Nicola Hein, Kai Winter and Sabine Worthmann, however, create the absolute opposite of such a remote closer (even if they certainly opened some remote desktop sessions during post-production and closed them with Ctrl + Alt + Del). In an act of physical multiplication they bring the listener music, full of sound narratives.
You could say that ‘Close Remote’ is anti-easy listening, as it allows absolutely no distraction and certainly no escape.
While Kaiser, Jun, Friedl, Hein, Winter and Worthmann approached us with the opener like a circling carrion vulture over our counted bodies, the second piece represents access. The instruments are now connected to us, or we to them. Although the set-up seems more airy than the first piece, as the sound space is brighter, the atmosphere is even more menacing, as no one in this place at this time can have any false ideas about where it will all lead. Hope is an illusion. Darkness is reality.
In ‘Remote Connectivity’, too, a glitch bursts into another dimension, from which the previously introduced ‘ES Stimme’ once again speaks, before a whole choir of ‘suffering voices’ rises up just a little later, voices that experience their incarnation from the orchestral interplay of the instruments.
The ideal introduction to the third piece, the longest on the release at 22 minutes, a confusing final act, as chaotic fragmentation and transparent dissolution interweave to form a Tibetan endless knot.
While the mood has been overwhelming so far, ‘Close Isolation’ now offers more time for active reflection on the sound experiences and their categorisation. The image of a landscape after a natural disaster offers itself as a visualisation, the tones are quieter but no less intense, sound impulses that you can hear the connection to sounds from the two previous pieces, less concrete relationships than additive qualities.
The stage is now brightly lit. Matthias Kaiser, Yan Jun, Reinhold Friedl, Nicola Hein, Kai Winter and Sabine Worthmann open the fourth wall, so to speak, of their ‘Close Remote’ production. We see without eyes what is left of the haunting threat. But we don't really know whether we have escaped unscathed, the myth of ‘Ninjutsu’ hovers over us as an ever quieter sound of eternal threat.
The title of the release, ‘Close Remote’, refers to the uncertainty in the run-up to the performance as to whether Chinese musician Yan Jun would be able to be physically present due to the even stricter visa regulations than usual during the pandemic. If he had not been allowed to enter the country, he would have been connected via Zoom. The extent to which this would have affected the performance is a matter for speculation, but his presence was definitely of great emotional significance and stimulating for the collective of musicians.
Thomas Venker,
2024.12.30.

whereisthezeitgeist?editing office.title: Der Tanz der Dämmerung黄昏之舞
whereisthezeitgeist?editing office.about:
"God's Burnout" is a trio comprising Saskia von Klitzing, Matthias Kaiser and Jun-Y Ciao. They premiered at this year's Moers Festival in Germany and subsequently performed at the REM Festival in Bremen. This recording was made in June of this year.
Saskia von Klitzing is the drummer for the renowned German rock band "Fehlfarben" and also for Caspar Brötzmann Massaker. Within "God's Burnout", she employs a barrel drum alongside an array of percussion instruments, including various cymbals, chains, and other objects. Matthias Kaiser, based in Cologne, is an accomplished violinist who has long been active within Germany's improvisational music scene, where he also serves as a dedicated organizer. He first met Jun-Y Ciao in 2011, and they have maintained a long-term collaborative relationship ever since.  "Where is the Zeitgeist? Editing Office" also released the duo album <The Rough Fabric of Inner Core> by Matthias Kaiser and Jun-Y Ciao this year. Several years prior, the German label Tonkunstmanufaktur published a trio album by Matthias Kaiser, Yan Jun, and Jun-Y Ciao, recorded in 2017, entitled <...Once We Run Out of Time. Storm Remains>. Having resided predominantly in Germany since last year, Jun-Y Ciao has increasingly focused his playing on high-register wind instruments such as the soprano saxophone, soprillo saxophone, and soprano suona in this recording. He has also incorporated greater use of found objects.
The entire recording unfolds in one continuous breath, developing within a poetic narrative. The album title < Der Tanz der Dämmerung>(it means :Dance of Twilight) seems to hint at something deeper. As dusk falls, the god of the sun slowly departs while the god of wine gradually takes center stage. Notes unfold within the gentle mist of twilight light, sounds shifting and unfolding within time that seems suspended. The entire album exudes a cool romanticism, reminiscent of Caspar David Friedrich's profoundly atmospheric paintings.

whereisthezeitgeist?editing office.title: Feedbacking:a number of feedback practices in China反馈中，一些在中国的反馈实践
whereisthezeitgeist?editing office.about:
The album « Feedbacking: a number of Feedback practices in China » , which has been in preparation for a year, is finally complete. The album contains the work of seventeen individuals and one group, including eight female musicians and fourteen male musicians . The album was initially titled « China Feedback», but I was prompted by Yan Jun to ask whether the use of the word ‘China’ was too grandiose. Indeed, at first, I only thought of emphasising the concept of geography to present a state of affairs by gathering artists and works that use feedback in China, but grandiose is not the original intention, nor is it possible to encompass all artists and works in China, and at the same time, I did not intend to make a conclusive collection, and it is perhaps too early to judge whether feedback, whether as a method or a concept, has already formed an independent phenomenon that can be explicitly described in China. So the title was changed to « Feedbacking », indicating a kind of ongoing process, which translates to « Feedbacking » in English, and the subtitle was added to indicate a geographical demarcation. I hope this is more objective and accurate, while still retaining the perspective of a group practice that can be observed and even studied under the concept of geography.
What is feedback? Simply, feedback is a fundamental concept in cybernetics, referring to the process of returning the output of a system to its inputs and altering them in some way, with a causal loop between them that affects the functioning of the system.
The principle of feedback is simple, but its presentation in the musical context is varied. Whether it is Jimi Hendrix or Alvin Lucier, David Lee Myers or Toshimaru Nakamura, these are all aspects of feedback that are presented in the context of individual concepts. That's probably what makes feedback so interesting, and you'll certainly find many different sides on this album. The simplicity of feedback is complicated by the complexity of its creator.
If feedback is like a musical instrument, it doesn't have a factory preset like a regular instrument, and it doesn't reveal a cultural root. A musical work that uses feedback is certainly not based solely on methodology; its formation process must be linked to the creator's ideas, whether emotional or rational, improvised or composed.
Therein lies the beauty of feedback.
(Jun-Y Ciao)

trackinfo.title: Fish, “Schroedinger’s Dobby”
trackinfo.about: The cat stayed with feedback in a locked room for five minutes. After that, the door and the windows were open back again. The feedback is gone while the cat remains there. Thanks to Little Dobby for the dedication.
trackinfo.credits: from Feedbacking:a number of feedback practices in China反馈中，一些在中国的反馈实践, released January 29, 2025

trackinfo.title: Li Jianhong，“The clumsy practitioner”
trackinfo.about:
Four years ago, sometime between summer and autumn, I recorded Feedback in the courtyard in the yard where I once lived. After moving to a new place, this project naturally carried on. My mother used to say“People, like birds”. For different reasons, I have moved to a lot of places in recent years. These recordings may be irrelevant for outsiders, but they mean a lot to me and my family.
This time, I played a Bansuri,which I'm not quite good at. Because I think the feedback of its air streams might be suitable for the environment of the courtyard.
trackinfo.credits: from Feedbacking:a number of feedback practices in China反馈中，一些在中国的反馈实践, released January 29, 2025

trackinfo.title: Li Qing，“Four-track major second solo”
trackinfo.about: High-gain low frequency feedback, triggered by the root note B and the major second C, which led to the drone sound with the interference between overtones.
trackinfo.credits: from Feedbacking:a number of feedback practices in China反馈中，一些在中国的反馈实践, released January 29, 2025

trackinfo.title: Li Song，“Walthamstow Marshes diary”
trackinfo.about:
I’ve started using snares and portable speakers to perform since 2021,sometime between spring and summer. Next year, I met Conal Blake and Regan Bowering. They are both musicians used to play drum or percussion. Therefore, we started doing performances together, using drums and other electronic devices. It’s all about snares, microphones, speakers and feedback.
This recording based on a composition in which we were experimenting the sound of a hanging snare drum. A clip mic and a Bluetooth amplifier were placed on different sides of the hanging snare. The feedback generated led to the vibration of snare. Then, the clip mic started to flap on the drum—revolving and jumping restlessly. At the end,I recorded this piece on a wild field out there near my home.
Recorded on a rainy day in April 2024, at Walthamstow Marshes, London.
trackinfo.credits: from Feedbacking:a number of feedback practices in China反馈中，一些在中国的反馈实践, released January 29, 2025

trackinfo.title: Li Weisi，“Acoustics”
trackinfo.about: Synopsis: I made a feedback system using a pair of headphones and a four-track tape deck. The sound is very gentle, and some very subtle movements that I made near the headphones disturbed the air and change the acoustic properties of the high frequencies of feedback . That's how the title got its name.
trackinfo.credits: from Feedbacking:a number of feedback practices in China反馈中，一些在中国的反馈实践, released January 29, 2025

trackinfo.title: MAI mai，“MAI mai sings Moon River”
trackinfo.about: MAI mai singing the classic interlude Moon River from the 1961 American movie Breakfast at Tiffany's through a vocoder. The oscillator inside the vocoder gave a fixed pitch so that MAI Mai's singing voice was always at the same pitch. Through the feedback mechanism within the vocoder, the voice is an expression of the song itself as well as a filter—the opening and closing of mouth affected the filter frequency—to modulate itself.
trackinfo.credits: from Feedbacking:a number of feedback practices in China反馈中，一些在中国的反馈实践, released January 29, 2025

trackinfo.title: Shanghai Oscillators Group（MAI mai，Yu，Jia Li，Yi Fan，Zhao Xiaoxiao， Jia Xiao），“Feedback Works NO.1”
trackinfo.about: This piece is based on a recording of a live performance of Shanghai Oscillator Group, with the feedback modulated by the mixer processed by Mai mai. The recording was modulated by a filter and a stereo delay effect, so as to generate the feedback within the mixer. This aurally blurred the gap between live performance and post production, as the sounds continuously feeding in and out of each other, like Ouroborous.
trackinfo.credits: from Feedbacking:a number of feedback practices in China反馈中，一些在中国的反馈实践, released January 29, 2025

trackinfo.title: Gogoj，“Gudong”
trackinfo.about: Electronic cello, effect pedal, compact guitar amp, Gu Dang, sometime around 4am. That's it, no more to say.
trackinfo.credits: from Feedbacking:a number of feedback practices in China反馈中，一些在中国的反馈实践, released January 29, 2025

trackinfo.title: Sun Yizhou，“Motivation”
trackinfo.about:
No-input feedback generated by the power amplifier. My operation was just connecting and disconnecting the circuit, and the sound changed without human intervention. Meanwhile, it was recorded with an Audio-Technica AT4021 microphone placed vertically on the speaker, as the electrical signal activated made the speaker generate kinetic energy to hit the microphone, and the gravity continuously pressed the microphone itself back against the speaker.
Recorded on March 22, 2024, Beijing.
trackinfo.credits: from Feedbacking:a number of feedback practices in China反馈中，一些在中国的反馈实践, released January 29, 2025

whereisthezeitgeist?editing office.title: Learning From Insects 师虫
whereisthezeitgeist?editing office.about:
Like many kids, I like to breed singing insects in my childhood. I self-taught wind instruments. One of my personal learning methods is to observe ways of singing of insects. Of course, this is not a simple imitation. For me, the vibration of tube reed is no different from the flapping of singing insects. From this perspective, all the insects are my teachers. I name all the tracks collected in this album after “vibration practice” to show my learning from these insects, in addition to some of my field recordings of singing insects.
2019, Shangai, Jun-Y Ciao

whereisthezeitgeist?editing office.title: Sang-Teh in Shanghai状态在上海
whereisthezeitgeist?editing office.about:
This situation. Sang Teh performance in Shanghai only 57 years! After, creation Seoul, then, 1961. (inspiration Ah Ahk heard everyday from Korean Broadcasting) 4 movements from the suite. I call it Situations : Now this title turning into chinees Zhang Tai. And they ar playing all-of-it-----14 movements. With your own wonderful indiginus instruments. , Tho, back-then, we did runthru at the National Music Institute, on the old Korean instruments (after concert our private pleshur organized by kayageum-virtuoso Hwang Byung-ki – old frend!) At concert used western instruments---but we playd like orientals! 2nd CD in this edition listen. Rough recording kept for years. Be heard also 4th movement: manytimes-playd by James Fulkerson’s Amsterdam-based ensembl ‘The Barton Workshop’. I look-forward after China exampl (a hope-for) that my music does get back to its land-of-origen, Korea. It coud sound as-well from Japan. And not-only with instruments ov your far-eastern cultursphere. The modern-western too. As we did. Indeed anything musical from any culture. (This germ-idea becom fulfilled in my recent Omniphony -intercultural co-operation. Invite many kinds to mix. Played for-the-first-time at that same Shanghai concert, recording destind for CD by Italian label ‘Setola di Maiale’.) Sequens-ov-tones In heterofony. Not to imitate the forms of another cultur But to learn-from. What iz apropriate. What iz right , and use-full.
Consider this composition as a realization of ideals setforth in my essay of-the-time (publishd in short-form in ‘Hangook Ilbo’) Of Ancient Times and Modern Sounds (printed-again, thistime in-full as a booklet to acompany the CD Crazy Musik: Ahk for Kwok by ‘What is the Zeitgeist’ a few years-ago. In China. And in chinese.) What is missing in the European model: refined exploration of timbre, textur, pitch-subtlty---evrything but the brikklike solids of precisely defined pitchplaces. Sound like mechanistic materializm? Every attempt at expressivity com-up against that limit. Pride in Harmony. But chords themselvs the limitingfactor, need to put lines together.
But only one line needed; one melody best. Free from the effects of excessiv civilization The tune’s tuning becomes subtil Ornamented nature continually resolving upon itself All-the-moreso when we all do it together. And this is an old-thing: the ethnomusicologysts call it “heterophony” (and for centurys we hyperrational snobs hav cryd !primitiv! as if somthing were missing that was never needed. Certainly i do-not lazily fall-bak on a borrowed pentatonic scale. Any of the 5-note scales. Not the 7s either. Nor any possibily less-than the 12. The note-sequences each different for each movement share the most-modern attainment of the complete twelvtone circle (known in China since befor-Pythagorus tho never used as-such) but not in any dogmatic-formula ov dodecaphony. Room for interval coherences: repeats, sequences, ear-garantees of shaped-perceptables. So does everything New turn-back to some-thing longtime-known. ?Has any innovation ever been anything but re-discovery.
Therfor any-number may play together. For me the first “indeterminacy”. (Yes, for-sur not the first-one:----think of John Cage. (But nowher-els like this one. I thank the Orient for that!)) The note-sequence (a “cantus firmus” if-yu-wil, is not the basis for conter-pointal additions but mor like basic asiatic-struturs (which i would later, much-later, find-out and learn, through playing with gamelan)……called “balungan” in Java and “pokok” in Bali). The note-sequens writ as letternames only. Which made easy re-write into chinese equivalence. This complemnted by short discription of the qualityz in-play. So it also first of the “text”compozitions, another newtecniqu to-be developd. Altho i then took “the oriental thing” further away from such formaltyz there is an aspect of later repetitiv music which also did, later, becom a part of my musical praxis. And this first composition uses indeterminacy in-any-way. So that makes-it a nother forward-step for me. 						 Its derivation of-it curious: First thought-----to simply lissen to them play as they added ornaments, improvised. I woud write--down. Try to write.down. I thought. But no-good. First-ov-all…..: dificult, Too dificult. Much-too-dificult. And anyway, woud inhibit performers trying-to-makesens of comlicated-and-unusual notation. Even more serius,,,,,,arbitrary. Against the nature of ornaments. Which shoudbe improvised. Best when spontaneous . based on direct feeling from context. We ar expanding the bounds of the definit, the definabl. Reasonabl coherens held. Evn when escape from too-rigid rationality. No less, this, than what we-can-see in traditional calligraphy…..I was imediatly “wow”ed when by the neon shop-signs……our troopship dockt in Yokohama. All my time in Korea i was staring at the writings-allaround which tho simple were wonderful. Evryday-utility, nothing-more. Yet infinitly beyutiful. This iz impossible in an alphabetic script-----as i found out later, much-later, trying to do it in english, writ with latinletters. Made to be incised in clay or stone, those scripts dissolv into nonverbal cursivs when pushd too-far. Why i said that “there is no calligraphy in he West, only handwriting. I hav,, all-my-life since then used a pen, hand writing wher the usual si som mechanic means. But----a blessing! since the pure-expresiv “meaningless” designs turn-into-meaning all-the-more as they become music. Dynamic flow to-match shape-of-sounds. The sighns may dissolv in longline patterns, suggestiv of melody. A new way to write a score. Drawing it. As the exact shape ov musicmoving. This i did when i returnd to America - from 1961. Pieces for strings as played for-exampl by Malcolm Goldstein (‘Pieces from the Past’, Pogus Productions) And ensembles (Chirographic played by Apartment House, in London. Setola di Maiale). And the ‘From the Judson Years’ CDs from Alga Marghen.
………………..flying white…………….... …….………..sonic silence……..……. And more. Ink Marks for Performance (much-played by Margaret Leng-Tan in her ‘East meets West’ concerts) ; getting wildly into the nature-of-the-game ,: Or you could just throw ink down on the paper (collaborate with artists: Geoff Hendrick’s class at Rutgers University , the score-designs as stage-decor). None-of-which possibl without the Far-Eastern exposur, calligraphy----just-enuf-study to liberate my hand. (Do-not test-me on traditional letters!) Thanks to my master, Kin Ki-Sung “sun saeng nim” Who gave-me the pen-name “Gwan Pok” - means “Contemplate Waterfall”. Which i like-to, somtimes, add to a characteristic IPh. In these pieces the players just “follow the lines” which-giv all the sonic information needed to dissolve the architectural bounds of civilized-behavior into richnesses of original-nature, now at-last (and as ever-befor) under a free&easy sensual-emotional controlled mindfullnes.
Philip Corner “Gwan Pok”			 August 2018

whereisthezeitgeist?editing office.title: The Rough Fabric of the Inner Core内核之绨
whereisthezeitgeist?editing office.about:
Let's start with the self-description of the two musicians behind “The Rough Fabric of the Inner Core / 内核之绨”, which they so generously shared with me: “Our music is harsh, radical, direct. The narration of the pieces is close to where the sounds originate, without cultivation or dressage. The playing on the instruments is the same: no sophisticated virtuosity, but what is created when handling the instruments is the source material. It's about the nucleus of music, the original power of sound.”
That sounds convincing at first. After all, this quickly explains the title of the release: “The Rough Fabric of the Inner Core / 内核之绨”.
But that's not quite true, of course. You don't even have to have heard the music; the cover alone, with its two sound bodies rotating around themselves and at the same time in dialogue with each other (which can of course be read as reduced, objectified artist surrogate bodies; one strikingly colored yellow, the other subtly pink), points to the special appeal of the encounter between Jun-Y Ciao and Matthias Kaiser.
We are dealing with two artistic personalities who are willing to engage in dialog, but not at any price. In other words, the sounds / noises they shared on the day of recording in Kaiser's home studio - Jun-Y Ciao performs with reeds whose vibrating sound is comparable to the sound production in harmonicas and accordions, Matthias Kaiser plays a processed violin - were only ever as innocent for a nanosecond, as the two of them put it in their quote, after which they were caught up in the centrifugal force of the two human-object bodies. Even if the six pieces that were created in “The Rough Fabric of the Inner Core / 内核之绨” were of course recorded in a linear fashion and left just as linear during production and mastering (by xx yy), the sketchy science fiction aesthetic of the cover drawn by Kaiser also refers to the potential of the music of Jun-Y Ciao / Matthias Kaiser to dissolve dimensions of time and space - what is created in one moment immediately becomes the (micro-causal) influence of itself in another (sound) dimension.
The delivery of the music to the author, a fascinating act of coded transmission. Six songs, tracks, whatever you want to call them, on the one hand minimally simply titled, on the other hand provided with additional numbers (Roman and Greek) in a maximally irritating way, which can almost be read as an artistic wink - in the sense of: of course everything is not as simple as it initially sounds. How could it be: the whole world is (not only at the moment) a giant cutter bucket, let's not even start with the universe.
But now finally into “The Rough Fabric of the Inner Core / 内核之绨”.
A sound interpretation in six acts.
1(III-2) - 10.20
The opener begins cautiously. In its best moments, music has the potential to turn sound spaces into associative real spaces. On “1(III-2)” - I'll use this cryptic abbreviation as the final title, it and the following tracks are too good to end up in the cutter bucket, to use the great Swabian word for garbage can again - we are presented with a view of a lonely hut in a remote area. A child screams - and initially gets our full attention. But then the sounds take over the room, at first you think they want to calm the agitated mood, but no, no: they want to cover it with noise. A tactic that usually (and also here) doesn't work - young parents and stumbling bullies know a thing or two about it.
2(I-1-c) - 23.11
Now we are standing in the yard. Suddenly the lonely hut has become a social group. What we hear at first sounds like a chorus of uncoordinated wild dogs. Noise vibrations that seem like a duet of generated sounds and field recordings - whereby the latter only spring from the imagination of the ears.
At 23 minutes and 11 seconds, the longest track on the release gives us a long breather in keeping with its length, in which the frequencies shyly cling to us like insects on an early summer's night. When we have long since heard the fade-out, Jun-Y Ciao / Matthias Kaiser once again give us particularly desperate sounds.
3(III-3) - 10.41
The most spherical piece of the release follows. “3(III-3)” sounds as if Jun-Y Ciao / Matthias Kaiser have set out to microscopically stretch the conceptually clear sound aesthetic of, say, Raster-Noton until the stretching creates a black sound hole - whose sound gives you commands that we would rather not put in writing here.
4(II-1-c) - 5.25
Nomen est omen, we have arrived at the core of “The Rough Fabric of the Inner Core / 内核之绨”. There is something diabolical in the air. There is a threat of losing control over one's own self. Not just for the two musicians. You feel as if you are listening to a piece as it realizes that it will never sound happy. It wails like a protagonist in a very, very old folk song, performed by a creature that has acquired the talent of imitation like a parrot. Absurd? Or at least confusing? Certainly. But who would have expected everything on “The Rough Fabric of the Inner Core / 内核之绨” to follow rational standards? That would be boring, wouldn't it?
5(I-2-C) - 8.09
We all know those country songs where someone plays the harmonica who can't, but we don't care, because the song lives from the fact that emotions are simply (as in not so simply) pressed into sounds. We listen to the sounds of the tears of a civilization that we have not yet discovered and are not at all sure that we ever want to.
6(III-4) - 5.37
At the end, things become earthly again. Matthias Kaiser's violin is exhibited with an almost overemphasized performative clarity (whereby the light feedback reinforces the grounding that the piece gives us). Jun-Y Ciao constantly fans new air into the room. A hand strokes our heads, a voice speaks reassuringly (without words): “Everything will be fine, you just have to start again at “1(III-2)” after “6(III-4)” and accept the cycle of things.”
It's 17.20 on April 19, 2025, VFB Stuttgart play Union Berlin in an hour, so there's still plenty of time for another centrifugal journey in “The Rough Fabric of the Inner Core / 内核之绨”. After that, everyone is left to their own devices, but nobody is fooling themselves.
Thomas Venker
2025.4

whereisthezeitgeist?editing office.title: Two Men's Trio
whereisthezeitgeist?editing office.about:
“两个人的三重奏”缘于我们两个人2017年在欧洲的巡演。在表演中，我们总是放置第三把椅子在我们之间。这把椅子上可以出现任何东西，当然也可以就是空着。
关于这个出版的起初，我们定下了规则：我们没有商量各自录三段录音，都是一遍过的整段录音，然后把它们合在一起，声相略分一下左中右，就有了新的空间。如果默契的话，草木、昆虫、人、山川、电梯，也都是这样接纳了对方的。
最终我们形成了两个版本，cd版是完整的、连续的；黑胶版是剪辑过的，打乱顺序的。两个版本的母带处理也不同。当然也就有了两种不同的结果。我们的确是在一遍又一遍地重新听着自己。
“Two men’s Trio” was based on our Europe Tour in 2017. We put always the third chair between us at the performance. It could be anything on this chair, or just leave it empty.
At the beginning of this publication，we have the rules for it: we do three recordings without discussing and listening to each other before, all one-takes separately tracks, then put them together by a little phase setting for being left, middle and right. a new space then formed. Plants, insects, human, mountains and rivers, and the elevators are all accept each other in this way, if they have rapport.
In the end, we have two versions here. On CD is it whole and continuous. On LP is it edited and also in different time order. Mastering methods are accordingly different, too, then there are two different results. Truly, we are re-listening to ourselves again and again.
